3.  Resolution Approving the Title VI Plan Relating to Section 5309 Funds
  As a condition of receiving federal grant funds the City must have an approved Title VI
  Plan which must be updated every three years.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt the resolution approving the updated City of Avalon Title VI Plan as it relates to
  federal funding.

4.  Ordinance Enacting Section 3-3.422 “Short-Term Rental Facilitator Reporting” to the
  Municipal Code
  This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived during the July 28,
  2026 regular City Council Meeting. The Short-Term Rental Facilitator Act of 2025 was
  enacted by Senate Bill 346 (Durazo). The Act provides a mechanism for cities to receive
  reporting regarding STRs operating in their jurisdiction. Once a city invokes the Act by
  ordinance, the Act requires online platforms like Airbnb and VRBO to identify and report
  short-term rentals in the city.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt the ordinance enacting Section 3-3.422 “Short-Term Rental Facilitator Reporting”
  to the Avalon Municipal Code.
GENERAL BUSINESS

5.  Planning Commission Appointments
  The terms for three (3) of the current Planning Commissioners expired on June 30, 2026.
  The City received six applications for the positions by the recruitment deadline. Mayor
  Marshall will provide her recommendations to the City Council at the meeting.
  Recommended Action
  1. Discuss applications received. 2. Consider the recommendation of Mayor Ann H.
  Marshall. 3. Make an appointment for three individuals to serve as Planning
  Commissioner for four-year terms expiring June 30, 2030. 4. Make an appointment for
  one individual to serve as Alternate Planning Commissioner for a two-year term expiring
  June 30, 2028.

AUGUST 4, 2026

6.  Civic Center Housing Project Feasibility Analysis
  —

  The City of Avalon continues to evaluate strategies to increase workforce and year-round
  housing opportunities consistent with the goals and policies outlined in the City’s 2021—
  2029 Housing Element. Goal V.C. and Policy V-16 identify the need to provide a variety
  of housing types, including workforce and seasonal employee housing, to support Avalon
  residents and employers.
  Recommended Action
  1. Receive the Civic Center Housing Project Financial Feasibility Analysis prepared by
  RSG; 2. Direct staff to not advance Phase 2 or Phase 3A; 3. Reject all bids received for
  Phase 3B and Phase 3C; 4. Direct staff to explore options to determine whether qualified
  nonprofit housing developers are interested in developing and operating the proposed
  housing project.

7.  ENGEO On-Call Engineering Services Contract Amendment
  On April 21, 2026, the City Council authorized the award of a professional services
  contract for on-call engineering, materials testing and inspection for an amount not-to-
  exceed $100,000 annually to ENGEO, Inc. for a three-year term. Since its authorization,
  the City has reached its annual expenditure limit.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute the First Amendment to the professional services
  agreement with ENGEO, Inc. for on-call engineering, materials testing and inspection
  increasing the contract total for the initial 12 month period May 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027
  —

  - by a total of $300,000 for a total not-to-exceed sum of $400,000.

8.  Advance Payment of Measure C Funds to the Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC)
  The Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC) has asked the City Council to approve
  execution of an agreement to provide an advance payment of approximately $654,753.60
  (including a State of California Administrative Fee described below) from the City’s
  general fund so that CIMC can participate in a Medicaid program to receive a substantial
  increase in funding.
  Recommended Action
  1. Approve the Intergovernmental Transfer (IGT) Agreement with the Department of
  Health Care Services (DHCS), which obligates the City to make an IGT transfer in the
  amount of approximately $654,753.60 (including a DHCS Administrative Fee described
  below) and subject to reconciliation by DHCS for Catalina Island Medical Center’s (CIMC)
  participation in the Voluntary Rate Range Intergovernmental Transfer Program, which
  CIMC believes will result in increased funding for CIMC. 2. Approve the transfer of
  approximately $654,753.60 to DHCS on or before November 20, 2026 in accordance with
  the IGT Agreement. 3. Approve an advance payment agreement with dM0, whereby
  CIMC would allow the City to offset the amount of the IGT transfer of $654,753.60 plus
  City Attorneys’ fees incurred in connection with the advance payment and certain
  administrative and lost opportunity fees, through Measure C funds, and, if necessary, any
  other available and permissible CIMC revenues over the course of eighteen months.

   I.  INTRODUCTION
“No person in the United States shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from
participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity
receiving Federal financial assistance” (42 U.S. C. 2000d)

The City of Avalon, as a recipient of federal financial assistance, will ensure full compliance with Title VI of
the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended and related statutes and regulations in the City of Avalon’s
Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project and the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Project. The City
will use Section 5309 federal funds for the construction and installation of passenger amenities and
improvements at the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal. The City of Avalon provides, without regard to race,
color, or national origin:

  •  Opportunities to participate in the transit planning and decision making processes; and,
  •  Fair decisions on the location of transit services and facilities.

These objectives are the basis for the City of Avalon’s Title VI Plan. The Plan that follows was updated in
conformance with FTA C 4702.1B-C (October 1, 2012). The new guidance in this circular integrates the
responsibilities to Limited English Proficient (LEP) Persons into programs and activities developed under
the Title VI regulations (49 CFR Part 21) to recipients of federal financial assistance.

The program contains all of the elements required in the U.S. Department of Transportation Federal
Transit Administration Title VI Circular dated October 1, 2012. It has been prepared using data from the
most recent 2010 U.S. Census.

The City Manager is responsible for ensuring implementation of the City of Avalon’s Title VI Plan. The
Public Works Director, on behalf of the City Manager, is responsible for the overall management of the
Title VI plan as outlined herein. The Public Works Director does not hereby assume responsibility for Title
VI compliance outside the scope of this report. The day to day administration of the Title VI Plan lies with
the Title VI Coordinator under the direct supervision of the Public Works Director.

In addition to the Title VI Coordinator, Title VI Specialists will be named in the following program areas:

2. Title VI Complaint Procedure

In order to comply with 49 CFR Section 21.9(b), the following complaint procedure will be followed by the
City of Avalon in the event that any person believes that he or she, individually, or as a member of any
specific class of persons, has been excluded form participation in, been denied the benefits of, or been
subjected to discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin with regard to:
 The opportunity to participate in the transit planning and decision making processes; and,
the right to fair decisions on the location of transit services, facilities and passenger amenities.

The complaint will be made in writing to the City of Avalon will include all information relevant to a
determination of discrimination. A complaint must be filed within 180-days after the alleged
discrimination. In case where the complainant is unable or incapable of providing a written statement, a
City of Avalon designee will, if necessary, assist the person in converting verbal complaints to writing and
will interview the complainant. The complainant or his/her representative will sign all complaints.

After review of the complaint, which will include, but not limited to, interviewing all appropriate City
personnel, the complainant, witnesses and review of the City’s policies and service standards, the City of
Avalon will make a determination of discrimination. If it is found that discrimination did not occur, the
complainant will be notified in writing and the procedure will be terminated. Notification will occur within
a reasonable time of the original submission of the complaint. At that time the complainant will be
advised of their right to challenge the City of Avalon by submitting a written request for a hearing within
five (5) days of the receipt of the determination.

If after the City of Avalon’s review of the complaint, it is found that discrimination may have occurred, a
formal hearing will be held. The complainant will be notified of this determination within reasonable time
of the submission of the complaint. The hearing will occur on an available and mutually agreed upon date
among both parties and will be attended by the City of Avalon, the complainant and the appropriate
personnel. Following the hearing, the City of Avalon will make a final determination. The complainant
will be notified of this determination in writing ten (10) business days of the hearing. If justified,
appropriate remedial action will be taken. The decision will be considered final at the City level.

If the Administrator finds that discrimination did not occur, the complainant will be notified of that
disposition and will advise the complainant of their right to submit their complaint to the Federal Transit
Administration for further investigation.

Complaint forms are available on the City of Avalon’s website. The forms are also available at the City of
Avalon City Manager’s office upon request. The general complaint procedure is available on the City’s
website. The detailed complaint procedure noted above will be made available to members of the public
upon request. Provisions will be made for persons with limited English proficiency.

  Ill.  Inclusive Public Participation
Avalon is committed to encouraging public participation for the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Project, as
community support is critical to the success of the project. The City has obtained Section 5039 federal
assistance for the construction and installation of passenger amenities and structural improvements for
the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal.

All residents of Avalon that use the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal, and all residents that will use and benefit
from the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project are encouraged to participate in the design
of the project. The City of Avalon will seek input from residents during significant phases of the project
and provide regular updates to the community and City Council as the Project moves through the design
and construction process.

Avalon’s public participation planning ensures that:

  •  Residents with concerns or interests will have an appropriate opportunity to participate in
  decisions about the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project, and will be notified of
  these opportunities to provide input.
   •  Community Involvement and contribution will be included in the development of the Project,
  passenger amenities and improvements to Cabrillo Mole.
  •  Concerns of all persons or groups participating in the process, uses of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry
  Terminal will be considered in Plan.
  •  Avalon will seek out and facilitate the involvement of those potentially impacted.

The Public Participation Plan outlines the importance of, and specific guidelines for, community
engagement. Included is the information about the value of public participation to the development of
the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project, the location and development of passenger
amenities and improvements at the Cabrillo Mole, and how it will be accomplished. It is important to
note that this Public Participation Plan will utilize a variety of communication mechanisms so all residents
will have the opportunity to participate.

  1. Opportunities for Public Participation

Numerous outreach methods will be used to gather community input and keep residents informed on
participation opportunities, as well as to inform residents of added infrastructure and improvements to
the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal, at project completion.

COMMUNITY MEETINGS
Community meetings will be scheduled at critical points during the project to allow for targeted
community input. A community meeting will be scheduled to allow the best opportunity for attendance
by the general public, and time most convenient to the general public. All community meetings will
include a presentation/update on the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project followed by a
question and answer session to ensure the participants are equally informed. The following will also be
considered in establishing the locations and scheduling times for community meetings:

  •  Convenience and accessibility for minorities, persons with disabilities, and LEP communities by
  hosting meetings in areas of the City that are accessible by public transit and near the
  development;
  •  Meetings hosted in ADA accessible buildings;
  •  Meetings scheduled at various times of the day/week to allow for residents to attend and
  participate, despite work and family obligations;
  •  Size of the venue and format of the meeting to allow for meaningful dialogue;
  •  Engaging meeting materials to facilitate participation.

MARKETING MATERIALS
Marketing materials notify the public of community meetings, project updates, and available Cabrillo
Mole Ferry Terminal Project passenger amenities upon project completion will be broadly advertised, in
order to seek community input and inform residents. Methods may include:

  •  Handouts distributed to key destinations in Avalon (English and Spanish) including City Hall,
  Avalon Public Library and Post Office Arcade;
  •  Flyers mailed to all box holders;
  •  City’s webpage www.cityofavalon.gov (English and Spanish);
  •  Social media conduits;
  •  Distribution of marketing materials to special interest and community groups, such as the Senior
  Center, Rotary Club, Lions Club, Women’s Forum and Chamber of Commerce;
   •  Notification of available translation services for persons with limited English proficiencies for
  meetings.

  2. Public Involvement Process

Measures taken will be targeted to overcome linguistic, institutional, cultural, economic, or other barriers
that may prevent minority and low income people and populations, persons with disabilities and persons
with limited English proficiency (LEP) from effectively participating in the development of the Cabrillo
Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project. By making a reasonable effort to include these populations,
Avalon hopes to ensure that the interests and input of all residents is given equal consideration, and that
the needs of the LEP population are addressed.

The City of Avalon’s Title VI Plan provided a Language Assistance Plan to encourage participation of LEP
individuals in the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project process, and notify LEP person of
opportunities to provide input.

  3. Next Steps

A complete record of public comments and input received from community meetings during the
development of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project will be summarized and presented
to the City Council; the public can access and download these City Council presentations at
www.cityofavalon.gov. City staff will also regularly update Council throughout the design of the Project.
Input gathered during the outreach process will be used by City staff in developing a preferred design
concept for the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal which will be presented to Council for consideration and
approval.

SUBJECT:  Ordinance enacting Section 3-3.422 “Short-Term Rental Facilitator
  Reporting” to the Municipal Code

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt the ordinance enacting Section 3-3.422 “Short-Term
Rental Facilitator Reporting” to the Avalon Municipal Code.

REPORT SUMMARY: This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived
during the July 28, 2026 regular City Council Meeting.

The Short-Term Rental Facilitator Act of 2025 was enacted by Senate Bill 346 (Durazo). The
Act provides a mechanism for cities to receive reporting regarding STRs operating in their
jurisdiction. Once a city invokes the Act by ordinance, the Act requires online platforms like
Airbnb and VRBO (defined in the statute as “short-term rental facilitators”) to identify and report
short-term rentals in the city. This information helps cities to identify STRs that operate
illegally, as well as to enforce their TOT ordinances and collect taxes that STR operators owe.

The Act expressly allows a city to require monthly reporting because the City requires TOT to
be remitted monthly.

The Act also expressly allows a city to establish administrative fines for reporting violations.
The proposed ordinance makes the reporting requirements under the Act a part of the City’s
STR ordinance; it makes violation of the reporting requirements an infraction; and it
establishes administrative fines of up to $5,000 per violation, in accordance with state law.
(Gov. Code § 53069.4, 36900(d).)

Adopting the proposed ordinance will require STR facilitators to report STRs in the City, which
will help the City to collect TOT and enforce the City’s STR regulations. This in turn will help
increase revenue to the City’s general fund and help protect public health, safety, and welfare.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW: Adoption of the proposed ordinance is exempt from the
California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) under Section 15378 because the activity is not
a “project” subject to CEQA. (Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 14, § 15378.) Section 15378 defines a
project as an activity that “has a potential for resulting in either a direct physical change in the
environment, or a reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment.” (Cal.
Code Regs. Tit. 14, § 15378(a).) These measures are not expected to result in any direct or
reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment, and thus adoption of the
ordinance is not a “project” under CEQA. Moreover, the City Council finds that even if adopting
this ordinance were considered a “project,” it is exempt from CEQA under State CEQA
Guidelines section 15061(b)(3), the “common sense” exemption, because it can be seen with
 certainty that there is no possibility that the Ordinance will have a significant effect on the
environment. (Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 14, §15061(b)(3).)

SUBJECT:  Civic Center Housing Project  —  Feasibility Analysis

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Receive the Civic Center Housing Project Financial Feasibility
Analysis prepared by RSG; 2. Direct staff to not advance Phase 2 or Phase 3A; 3. Reject all bids
received for Phase 3B and Phase 3C; 4. Direct staff to explore options to determine whether
qualified nonprofit housing developers are interested in developing and operating the proposed
housing project.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City of Avalon continues to evaluate strategies to increase workforce
and year-round housing opportunities consistent with the goals and policies outlined in the City’s
2021—2029 Housing Element. Goal V.C. and Policy V-16 identify the need to provide a variety
of housing types, including workforce and seasonal employee housing, to support Avalon
residents and employers.

To address these needs, the City identified publicly owned property adjacent to the Avalon Civic
Center as a potential site for development. City Staff modeled and developed a 26-unit modular
workforce housing project consisting of: (6) studio efficiency units, (10) one-bedroom units; and
(10) two-bedroom units.

In December 2024, the City Council authorized issuance of a Request for Proposals (RFP”) for
development of the Project. The RFP contemplated the following process, and updates to this
process are included below:

Phase 1: Pre-construction design, engineering, planning, and cost refinement; and
Phase 2: Manufacturing, delivery, and installation of modular housing units.

On May 6, 2025, the City Council authorized an agreement with US-Offsite to complete Phase
1 services. As part of that process, the City retained RSG to evaluate development structures,
management models, and financial feasibility associated with the Project.

On December 15, 2025, the City published RFPs for Phase 3A: Site Preparation and 3B:
Modular Unit Construction. On March 17, 2026 City Council rejected bids on 3A and approved
reissuing 3B (due to receiving no qualified bids). On March 24, 2026 the City published RFPs
for 3B: Delivery and Setting of Modular Units and 3C: Post Setting (formerly combined into 3B).

On April 23, 2026, the City received qualified bids for both reissued Phase 3B and 3C.
 RSG’s financial feasibility analysis concluded that while the proposed Project may generate
sufficient operating income to cover ongoing operational expenses, the Project remains
financially constrained due to high development costs relative to anticipated rental revenues.

Key findings from the analysis include:
  • Estimated total development cost of approximately $10.7 million;
  • Estimated construction cost of approximately $410,758 per unit;
  • Projected annual gross rental revenue of approximately $864,000;
  • Stabilized net operating income of approximately $471,169;
  • Initial debt service coverage ratio (“DSCR”) of approximately 1 .01; and
  • Development yield of approximately 4.4%, below typical market feasibility thresholds.

RSG noted that conventional multifamily lenders generally require a minimum stabilized DSCR
of approximately 1 .20 and that market-rate multifamily projects in Los Angeles County generally
target development yields near 6.0%.

The analysis concluded that the Project would likely be infeasible for a private market-rate
developer without public subsidy or alternative financing structures. While the City may consider
alternative underwriting standards due to its policy objectives, RSG emphasized that the
proposed Project may present financial risk to the City’s General Fund if revenues, occupancy,
or operating assumptions do not perform as projected.

Development and Operational Risk
The feasibility analysis further outlines substantial risks associated with the City acting as
developer, lender, equity partner, asset manager, and/or property manager.

Should the City proceed as developer, the City would assume responsibility for:
  • Construction oversight and project management;
  • Budget and schedule management;
  • Insurance and contingency funding;
  • Regulatory compliance;
  • Ongoing asset management; and
  • Day-to-day property management operations.

In addition, the City would be responsible for the future maintenance obligations, and long-term
capital replacement requirements. While none of these items is a complete deterrent to the City
initiating this project, combined with the existing interest rate market the current risks are too
high.

Although a long-term ground lease structure with a third-party developer could reduce some
financial and operational risks, the analysis notes that such a structure would likely trigger
compliance with the California Surplus Land Act (‘SLA”), potentially extending timelines and
limiting flexibility regarding workforce housing objectives.

RSG also indicated that developer interest in the site may be limited due to current construction
costs, project scale, and the competitive nature of affordable housing financing programs.
 Capital Improvement Priorities
In addition to the financial risks identified in the feasibility analysis, the City is currently
undertaking or preparing for several major capital infrastructure investments, including:
  • Cabrillo Ferry Terminal Project
  • Five Corners Utility & Traffic Safety Improvement Project
  • Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site Optimization Project
  • Pebbly Beach Revetment and Roadway Project
  • South Beach Restoration Project

These projects represent significant long-term infrastructure and financial commitments that are
critical to maintaining essential public services and operational resiliency throughout the
community. Although all the foregoing projects are tied to grant funding, the City will experience
a financial lag before receiving reimbursement for grant funded expenses. This liquidity risk must
be acknowledged and conservatively managed.

Given the scale of these existing obligations, proceeding with the Civic Center Housing Project
without substantial outside grant funding, subsidy, or development participation could place
additional strain on City financial resources and staffing capacity.

Staff is actively engaged in pursuing alternate funding sources for this Project by way of Federal
Earmarks and state and county grant opportunities. Staff is confident that funding options will
present themselves in the near future and this project will be able to advance to the next stage
soon.

Accordingly, staff recommends the City defer advancement of Phase 2 and Phase 3A (and
additional phases) until outside funding sources are identified and secured sufficient to
substantially reduce risk exposure to the General Fund and to reject all bids received for Phase
3B and 3C pursuant to AMC 3-4-206 (d) Rejection of Bids.

OPTION: Staff recommends exploring options to evaluate market interest from qualified
nonprofit or mission-driven housing developers, including but not limited to, the issuance of a
Request for Information (“RFI”).

  The purpose of the RFI would be to:
  • Assess developer interest in the site;
  • Identify potential partnership structures;
  • Evaluate alternative financing approaches;
  • Determine whether a third-party entity could assume development, asset
  management, and property management responsibilities; and
  • Explore opportunities to maintain City land ownership through a ground lease or
  similar disposition structure.

The RFI process could provide the City with additional information regarding potential
development partnerships while preserving flexibility and minimizing immediate financial
commitments.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: At this time, no additional fiscal appropriation is recommended.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Not applicable.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Council action could
potentially increase near-term financial risk.

proposed housing project on publicly owned property adjacent to the Avalon Civic

This memorandum summarizes key factors affecting development risk, operational
responsibility, and long-term financial sustainability, while supporting the City’s goal
of retaining public ownership of the site. The scenarios outlined below identify
potential risks, mitigation strategies, and benefits associated with different project
disposition, development, and management structures. The memorandum also
discusses how these scenarios interact with the Surplus Land Act (“SLA”).

The scenarios evaluated include:

  development phase and contracting asset and property management to a
  third-party, or
  •  Ground-leasing the site to a third-party.

DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT STRUCTURES

The development and management structure of a housing project will influence the
allocation of development responsibilities, operational oversight, and long-term
financial performance. At a high level, the City must determine how development,
asset management, and day-to-day property management responsibilities will be
structured while maintaining its priority of retaining public ownership of the site.
These responsibilities may be carried out directly by the City or delegated to third-
party partners depending on the selected development and management approach.

To help evaluate these options, this section outlines the key roles involved in project
development and ongoing housing operations, including their respective
responsibilities and areas of risk. The section also describes potential housing
management structures that could be used to operate the property and maintain
long-term financial and operational sustainability.

Roles and Responsibilities

The successful development and long-term operation of the Project will require
distinct specializations that support planning, construction oversight, financial
performance, and day-to-day property management. Each role carries specific
responsibilities that contribute to the overall feasibility and sustainability of the
Project. The following sections describe the primary functions of the developer,
asset manager, and property manager and how each contributes to the Project’s
success.

Developer
Developers are responsible for coordinating all stages of project delivery and must
have financial, project management, and technical planning and construction
expertise. At the initiation of a project, the developer evaluates the feasibility of the
project and establishes a development plan. Effective project management and the
ability to adapt to changing conditions are essential to maintaining the project
schedule and budget. Delays and cost increases can directly impact the financial
feasibility of development. The developer is responsible for actively planning to limit
and manage project delays through scheduling, budgeting, and value engineering
perspectives. Finally, developers need technical knowledge of the general plan and
planning code, as well as the ability to monitor quality standards and safety
regulations during the vertical construction stage.

Asset Manager
An asset manager provides long term oversight to protect the owner’s investment
and ensure the property performs as intended. The asset manager is focused on
financial planning, risk management, and maintaining the value of the development
over time. The asset manager monitors operating revenues and expenses,
manages reserve funds, and evaluates insurance needs. They also ensure
compliance with regulatory requirements and guide capital improvement planning

Asset managers may also be involved in scheduling and oversight of large scale
capital improvements to the property. Effective asset management helps stabilize
operations, extend the useful life of the property, and support the financial
sustainability of the project.

Property Manager
A property manager oversees the day-to-day operations of the property and its
relationships with tenants. This includes maintaining a safe, habitable rental
property, leasing, rent collection, and oversight of maintenance and repairs.
Additionally, property managers administer tenant eligibility requirements, if
applicable, and maintains compliance with relevant housing regulations. The
property manager’s work directly affects the reputation and long-term performance
of the property. Property managers may also be the liaison between the asset
manager and tenants, especially when capital improvements are necessary.
Effective property management requires clear communication with tenants, timely
response to maintenance needs, and coordination with the owner and asset
manager to plan for ongoing building upkeep.

City As Developer
If the City acts as the developer, it will assume responsibility for coordinating the
completion of the Project and managing associated risks. Before proceeding with
Phase 2 of the Project, the City should evaluate its internal project management
capacity and identify staff to oversee construction, contract administration, and
schedule coordination. The City will also need to review the financial feasibility of
the Project and establish a budget that accounts for potential delays, cost changes,
and insurance requirements. When the City acts as the primary equity investor, the
financial return requirements are likely to be different from those expected by
private, market-rate developers. In this scenario, the City’s investment objectives
may focus more on policy goals or public benefits rather than maximizing profit. As
a result, the City may accept lower financial returns compared to private developers,
prioritizing community outcomes, affordability, or other strategic objectives
associated with the project. In addition, the City should plan to engage qualified
third-party asset management and property management firms to support ongoing
operations once the Project is complete.

Retaining legal advice to review contracts for clarity and setting up pro-active
compliance procedures will lower risk for the Project. This may require special
counsel. The City will need to be prepared to follow procurement requirements or

Ground Lease to Third Party
A ground lease is a common approach used by cities to reduce direct financial and
construction risk while retaining ownership of the land. Under this model, the City
leases the site to a private developer who is responsible for financing, constructing,
and operating the housing. The City may also act as the primary equity investor,
simplifying the financial capital stack. The structure brings development expertise
and shifts costs and delivery risks to the private developer, while the City maintains
land ownership.

Because the developer assumes responsibility for project delivery and performance,
the City has less direct control over unit design, leasing practices, and long-term
operational decisions unless these are defined in the ground lease agreement and
associated regulatory documents. Clear contract terms and review by legal counsel
are necessary to establish expectations, insurance requirements, and performance
standards.

The City would continue to monitor compliance with the ground lease but would have
limited involvement in day-to-day construction oversight or property operations. A
long-term ground lease would require the City to follow the Surplus Land Act (“SLA”)
process if the lease term exceeds 15 years. Typical ground lease terms range from
30 to 99 years. The SLA includes required noticing and negotiation periods, which
may affect the project schedule and feasibility depending on market interest and
timing considerations.

Surplus Land Act Considerations
The California Surplus Land Act (“SLA”) governs the disposition of publicly owned
land and prioritizes its use for affordable housing development. A ‘disposition” under
the SLA includes the sale of public land or entering into a ground lease longer than
15 years, including extension options, as defined in Government Code Section
54221(d). If the City pursues a long-term ground lease for the site, the Project would
likely be subject to the SLA process.

Under the SLA, the City must issue a Notice of Availability to eligible entities,
including affordable housing developers and certain public agencies. These entities
have 60 days to express interest in the site. If interest is received, the City must
engage in a minimum 90-day good-faith negotiation period with interested parties.
The City must also provide documentation to the California Department of Housing
and Community Development demonstrating compliance with the SLA before
completing a disposition.

If mulUple eligible developers express interest, the City is generally required to
prioritize proposals that provide the greatest number of affordable housing units at
the deepest levels of affordability, consistent with the intent of the SLA to maximize

FINANCIAL FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS

RSG’s financial feasibility analysis evaluates the proposed 26-unit multifamily
development based on current construction costs, market-rate revenue
assumptions, operating expenses, and multifamily financing benchmarks. The
analysis indicates that the Project can generate sufficient operating income to cover
ongoing expenses but remains financially constrained due to high development
costs and relatively modest rental revenues. With a total estimated construction cost
of approximately $10.7 million, the Project achieves a stabilized net operating
income that exceeds projected debt service, but results in a marginal initial debt
service coverage ratio and a development yield below market thresholds. While
these metrics suggest the Project would be infeasible for a private developer, the
City’s dual role as lender and equity partner, along with its broader policy objectives,
provides flexibility to consider alternative underwriting standards when evaluating
overall feasibility and risk. However, the proposed Project poses significant risk to
the City’s General Fund if the Project does not perform as expected.

Source of Funds, Debt Service Coverage, and Development Yield

Based on RSG’s experience and recent discussions with developers and real estate
investors, market rate multifamily developments typically have a capital stack that
includes approximately 50% debt and 50% equity. Based on conversations with City
staff, the City expects to be both the lender and equity partner for the Project. RSG
assumed that the debt would cover half of the total construction costs, with
amortization of 20 years, and 6.25% interest rate.

Based on these assumptions, the annual debt service is $468,366 and with annual
net operating income of $471,169, the Project has a debt service coverage ratio of
1.01, meaning that the net operating income is about 1% higher than the annual
debt service payment. Conventional lenders generally require a minimum debt
service coverage ratio of 1 .20 for stabilized multifamily. This debt service coverage
ratio represents a market-based metric for acceptable level of risk, meaning that
debt service coverage ratios below 1.20 indicate a higher risk of loan payment
default. Because rental income escalates annually and loan payments are static,
over time the debt service coverage ratio is projected to improve, with the average
debt service coverage ratio over the 20-year term at about 1 .30. The City is not a
conventional lender, however, and may consider alternative minimum debt service
coverage ratio thresholds.

RSG considered a second benchmark that multifamily developers utilize to evaluate
the feasibility of proposed developments, the development yield. Developers
measure yield by dividing the net operating income into the development cost. Yield
on cost for new development is similar to the capitalization rate for a stabilized real
estate asset, but yields are generally higher than capitalization rates to account for
the additional risks of new development. Current market yields for multifamily in Los
Angeles County are 6.0%, meaning that developers would be unlikely to move
forward with a development that has a yield lower than 6.0%. RSG calculated the
yield for the proposed Project to be 4.4%, meaning that the Project would likely be
infeasible for a private developer. The City, however, does not have traditional
investors with minimum required returns and may consider an alternative minimum
yield threshold.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Approve the Intergovernmental Transfer (IGT) Agreement
with the Department of Health Care Services (DHCS), which obligates the City to make an IGT
transfer in the amount of approximately $654,753.60 (including a DHCS Administrative Fee
described below) and subject to reconciliation by DHCS for Catalina Island Medical Center’s
(CIMC) participation in the Voluntary Rate Range Intergovernmental Transfer Program, which
CIMC believes will result in increased funding for CIMC. 2. Approve the transfer of
approximately $654,753.60 to DHCS on or before November 20, 2026 in accordance with the
IGT Agreement. 3. Approve an advance payment agreement with CIMC, whereby CIMC would
allow the City to offset the amount of the IGT transfer of $654,753.60 plus City Attorneys’ fees
incurred in connection with the advance payment and certain administrative and lost
opportunity fees, through Measure C funds, and, if necessary, any other available and
permissible CIMC revenues over the course of eighteen months.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC) has asked the City Council
to approve execution of an agreement to provide an advance payment of approximately
$654,753.60 (including a State of California Administrative Fee described below) from the
City’s general fund so that CIMC can participate in a Medicaid program to receive a substantial
increase in funding.

The Medicaid program (called “Medi-Cal” in California) is jointly funded by the State of
California and the federal government for certain residents of the State. The State’s share of
the funding is a combination of State funds appropriated to DHCS, public funds transferred
from other public agencies such as cities or counties (called “Intergovernmental Transfer” or
“IGT”), and certain health care-related taxes. These funds together represent the “non-federal
share” of the funding to pay for Medi-Cal program expenses and are used to draw down
matching federal funds.

The specific program that CIMC wants to participate is called the Voluntary Rate Range
Intergovernmental Transfer Program. It was established in 2011-2012 to allow local public
“transferring entities” to contribute their own funds via IGTs to help DHCS to pay capitation
rates to Medi-Cal managed care plans at the upper bound of the rate range and to draw down
matching federal funds based on those higher rates. The plans must use the “rate range
increases” (that is, the difference between the lower bound and the upper bound of the range)
to make increased payments to health care providers to increase access to services for their
Medi-Cal enrollees.
